## **Mandatory 8D and CAPA Requirements and Adoption Scale by Industry**

The Eight Disciplines problem-solving method (8D), originating in Ford Motor Company's Team Oriented Problem Solving (TOPS) program established in 1987 and later developed into Global 8D, added the D0 preparation gate and escape-point analysis across D4-D6. It has evolved from an internal automotive process into a standard structure for corrective and preventive action (CAPA) across global industry1. However, the legal force and scope of 8D differ significantly among manufacturing industries according to quality management system (QMS) standards, customer-specific requirements (CSR) and government regulation2. The substantial structural gap between contractual targets (DEADLINE) and actual measured factory cycle times (MEASURED) arises from the dual operating nature of 8D and CAPA: immediate containment (D0-D3) moves on an emergency hourly timescale to protect the customer's production line, while experimental root-cause analysis (D4), design or process changes (D5-D6), and statistical effectiveness validation across multiple production batches (D7-D8) depend on physical cycles and cross-functional approval constraints2.<br>
In automotive manufacturing, structured problem solving is mandatory under **IATF 16949:2016**, clause 10.2.3 on problem solving, and IATF certification Rules 6th Edition, effective 1 January 2025. Organizations must maintain a documented process covering interim containment, root-cause analysis, systemic corrective action and effectiveness verification, and use the format and method specified by the customer2. Most IATF original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), including Ford Motor Company, General Motors (GM), Stellantis (FCA US / FCA Italy), Volkswagen Group, BMW Group, Daimler AG (Mercedes-Benz), Geely Group, IVECO Group and Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), together with Tier-1 suppliers such as Continental AG, Grupo Segura, KSR International and Novares, directly require 8D reports in their CSRs and supplier-quality portals5. Official IATF Global Oversight measurements show **93,908** certified sites on 31 January 2024, increasing to **98,803** on 20 January 2025, **99,686** on 20 February 2025, **101,024** on 20 June 2025, **101,407** on 20 July 2025, and **104,216 manufacturing sites** worldwide on 20 December 2025, up from only 374 in 2002. North America accounts for 6,431 sites, or 6.17% of the global total, including 3,693 in the United States and 2,327 in Mexico18. The original report describes all 104,216 plants and sub-tier suppliers developing toward IATF compliance under clause 8.4.2.3 as subject to the 8D process18.<br>
In aerospace and defence, 8D is standardized and mandated through **SAE AS13000**, *Problem Solving Requirements for Suppliers*, and the integrated **SAE AS13100**, accompanied by reference manual **RM13000**, *8D Problem Solving Methods*, issued on 8 March 2021 and revised on 8 December 2023, as approved by Aerospace Engine Supplier Quality (AESQ)25. AS13000 requires suppliers in the aerospace-engine supply chain, including major groups such as Safran Group and Barnes Aerospace and their subcontractor networks, to use the nine-step D0-D8 form and process when responding to customer corrective-action requests, regardless of customer identity25. The original report also associates the US defence sector's 8D structure with military standard **MIL-STD-1520C**, *Corrective Action and Disposition System for Nonconforming Material*, and comparable Supplier Corrective Action Request (SCAR) processes used by contractors such as Lockheed Martin / Derco Aerospace5. Available published data provide no measured worldwide count of sites independently meeting AS13000/AS13100 or MIL-STD-1520C.<br>
In electronics and semiconductors, the original report identifies **JEDEC JESD671**, *Component Quality Problem Analysis and Corrective Action Requirements* (JEDEC 671), and its mandatory reference in the Automotive Electronics Council's **AEC-Q100 Rev J** for automotive semiconductors as the basis for standardized 8D requirements10. It lists STMicroelectronics, with its global network of ISO/IEC 17025 failure-analysis laboratories, Sony Semiconductor Solutions, Silicon Labs, Skyworks Solutions (form SQ04-0372 in handbook SQ02-0020), Texas Instruments, Samsung Semiconductor and Integrated Silicon Solution (ISSI) as requiring 8D for customer complaints and batch defects10. Apart from automotive semiconductor plants included in the 104,216 IATF 16949 sites, no separately measured global count of semiconductor plants applying JESD671 is available22.<br>
For medical devices and pharmaceuticals, regulators do not mandate the term "8D" in legislation but require a technically comparable structured **CAPA** process; many companies use 8D forms for root-cause investigation6. In medical devices, **FDA 21 CFR 820.100**, described in the original research as transitioning to the **Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR)** aligned with **ISO 13485 clause 8.5**, and **EU MDR Article 10(9)** require manufacturers to establish systems for root-cause investigation, corrective/preventive action and effectiveness verification before closure39. In pharmaceuticals, deviation management and CAPA are governed by Good Manufacturing Practice requirements, **FDA cGMP / GxP**6. Rail, appliances and contract manufacturing / EMS apply 8D through OEM contractual requirements (SCAR) based on **ISO 9001 clause 10.2**, without a separate industry-wide mandatory 8D standard or official counts of adopting sites45.

## **Actual Cycle Times and Deadlines by Industry**

Comparing OEM contractual deadlines (DEADLINE) with measured cycle times (MEASURED) from academic studies and industry surveys reveals a systematic gap. The original report describes OEM quality manuals as requiring completion within **10 working days to 40 calendar days**, while citing full problem-solving cycles, from complaint receipt through effectiveness validation and closure, of **39-63 calendar days** in manufacturing and **116-379 calendar days** in medical devices, with a **395-calendar-day / 13-month median**8. These original headline claims must be read with the corrections and sample-data exclusions in the companion synthesis.<br>
![][image3]

### **1. Automotive**

Although no single multi-company survey provides an industry-wide measured average, the original report attributes specific factory measurements to peer-reviewed automotive component studies. It reports a baseline mean of **63 calendar days** for the full D1-D8 cycle, reduced to **41 calendar days** after standardization, a 34.9% improvement or 22 days saved48. Another case study, described here as published in 2024, concerns "cover pillar loop scratch" defects on automotive seat-belt line SB3. The 8D implementation reduced scrap from 47 units in February 2020 and 60 in March 2020 to zero in July 2020 over approximately **120 calendar days / 4 months**, while reducing ramp-up time from **20 to 2 days** and model-changeover time from **600 to 102 minutes**1. A 2019 study combining Quick Response Quality Control (QRQC) and 8D for contamination and pitting on painted metal rails, report 6102-3339 with ![][image1] defective painted rails and ![][image4] defective raw rails, recorded **12 calendar days** between component production on 18 September 2019 and detection at the customer line plus initial 8D analysis on 30 September 2019. It reported average defects declining from 4.6 to 2.4 after D8 closure48.<br>
Compared with the cited 41-63-day cycles, automotive OEM and Tier-1 manuals set much shorter DEADLINE milestones to protect assembly lines. **Ford Motor Company** CSRs require an initial response, emergency action, containment at Ford and certified shipments (D0-D3) within **24 hours**; notification to Ford Customer Service Division (FCSD) within **48 hours** if service parts may be affected; and a full 8D report or six-panel Six Sigma report, including a preliminary or verified root cause and evidence-supported corrective/preventive action plan, within **15 calendar days**2. **General Motors**, through *GM 1927* and *Quality Systems Basics (QSB)*, specifies Fast Response using a Practical Problem Solving Report (PPSR / 8D): containment D3 within **24 hours**, root cause D4 within **7 calendar days**, corrective-action implementation D5-D6 within **14 calendar days**, and D8 closure targeted at **30 calendar days**, with a maximum of **40 calendar days**49. The original report attributes to **Volkswagen Group**, *Formel Q Konkret* 6th Edition of October 2021 and 7th Edition of 30 March 2025, acknowledgement and initial containment D3 within **24 hours** or the next working day, and full 8D completion within **10 working days**52. The companion synthesis corrects the last distinction: in the 6th edition, 10 working days concerns the long-term measure update; final completion is 20 working days.<br>
Tier-1 deadlines follow a similar structure. **Continental AG**, in its Supplier Requirements Manual and General Quality Agreement *QPR A2C00052917AAA*, requires acknowledgement of nonconformity and a containment plan within **24 hours**, formal communication of **D1, D2 and D3 within 2 working days**, and an expert meeting or Continental site visit within **48 hours** if escalation results in controlled-shipping status CSL1/CSL215. **Grupo Segura**, Supplier Quality and Development Manual of February 2026, requires a containment plan and 8D through **D3 in under 24 hours**, a report through **D5-D6 within 3 days**, and full **D8 closure within 10 days**16. **KSR International**, Supplier Handbook of July 2023, specifies **24 hours / 1 working day** for containment D3 and **14 working days** for corrective action / 8D17. **Novares Group** (2018) and **Emerge** (Issue 8) both require a D3 containment plan within **24 hours** of the request13. For IATF 16949 certification audit nonconformities, the original report describes IATF Rules 5th and 6th Editions as requiring the certification body to issue the final report within **15 calendar days** and the company to complete corrective-action implementation within **90 calendar days** after the closing meeting14; the companion synthesis clarifies the certification body's 90-day decision deadline versus the company's submission deadlines. Separately, software vendor **Jodoo** (VENDOR CLAIM) states that digitizing automotive and electronics 8D reduced average closure time from **18 to 11 days**. It also cites a supplier averaging **21 days** against an internal **10-day** target, and a D7 effectiveness window of **30 days** with zero recurrence across three production runs46. Practitioner ESTIMATE ranges are **24-48 hours** for containment and **30-60 days** for full closure2; **3-30 days**, including a **10-working-day** full-report deadline for a 2.5-hour line stoppage involving 14 cracked welds in a 1,200-unit batch5; or **10 days** for an interim report and **45 days** for final closure66.

### **2. Aerospace / AS13000 and Defence**

**No industry-wide MEASURED average 8D closure time** is available in the reviewed scientific publications. The process-control reference RM13006 mentions a mean time between equipment failures of 7.7 days, which is not an 8D closure cycle26. Instead, aerospace and defence rely on strict DEADLINE milestones under **SAE AS13000** and prime-contractor SCAR requirements. **Barnes Aerospace**, Supplier Quality Requirements under AS13000 dated October 2023, requires immediate containment, a D3 results report within **24 hours**, and an AS13000-format 8D corrective-action plan within **30 calendar days**3. **Safran Group**, in its AS13000 quality requirements, requires immediate containment **S0/D0 within 2 days / 48 hours**29. **Lockheed Martin / Derco Aerospace**, Supplier Quality Manual QA100-102 revised on 24 February 2021, requires notification of nonconformities potentially affecting flight safety within **24 hours** of discovery, and other suspected or confirmed nonconformities within **5 working days**30. For final D8 closure, the standardized AS13000-format process cited by the report treats 8D as closed after **3 consecutive defect-free deliveries** following corrective action, written customer approval, or **30 calendar days** after submission without a customer request for additional information67.

### **3. Electronics and Semiconductors**

There is **no broad-survey MEASURED industry-wide average** for electronics or semiconductor manufacturing. A peer-reviewed 2023 case involving leakage current and temperature-sensor failures caused by flux residue, investigated using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), reported that a Lean 8D analysis form reduced a specific analysis activity from **several working days manually to 30 minutes**. The original report also cites a total-cycle reduction from **63 to 41 days**47. A 2025 MDPI study applying Ford 8D to a shipment of 300 defective semiconductor components, representing 100% of the shipment at the customer line, did not publish a large-sample mean duration68.<br>
A distinctive semiconductor constraint is physical laboratory failure analysis: SEM, transmission electron microscopy (TEM), focused ion beam (FIB) and electrical fault localization performed by failure-analysis engineers before quality engineers complete the 8D documentation. The original report links these DEADLINE expectations to **JEDEC JESD671**10. **Silicon Labs** publishes four milestones in **working days**: initial failure analysis within **7 working days** of receiving a suspected defective component (RMA); 8D containment D3 within **5 working days** after notifying the customer or confirming failure following preliminary analysis; final failure analysis within **22 working days** of receiving the suspected component; and an 8D root-cause/corrective-action plan D4-D5 within **14 working days** after customer notification or root-cause identification following final analysis10. The report attributes this sequence to JESD671 and its references in **AEC-Q100 Rev J** and **ISSI** documentation; the companion synthesis notes that the Silicon Labs FAQ itself does not substantiate that standards connection. Adding 22 working days for final analysis and 14 for D4-D5 yields **36 working days**, approximately **50 calendar days**, before D6-D8 implementation and effectiveness validation. **Skyworks Solutions** manual SQ02-0020 notes that those later stages can take longer depending on complexity10. In high-speed electronic cable assembly, including Twinax under JEDEC J-STD-020, **Xdpigo** states that D3 containment begins within **48 hours** for a confirmed manufacturing defect, with standard RMA review within **30 calendar days** of receipt69. **Chartered Semiconductor** provides a practitioner ESTIMATE of **60-90 calendar days** for complete 8D closure including horizontal prevention D7-D870.

### **4. Medical Devices / CAPA**

Medical devices are the only sector in this review with large-scale, multi-site empirical MEASURED data from the **Medical Device Innovation Consortium (MDIC)**, published in the *Make CAPA Cool* whitepaper (2022/2023)9. MDIC measured hundreds of actual CAPAs before and after risk-based process redesign. The original report gives **Baseline CAPAs, sample ![][image5], MEASURED**, a mean overall cycle from detection to closure of **379 calendar days**, over 12.5 months, comprising mean initiation of **43 days**, implementation of **131 days** and closure/effectiveness checks of **221 days**9. It gives **Pilot: External CAPAs, sample ![][image6], MEASURED**, for serious externally reportable issues, a mean overall cycle of **167 calendar days**, with **12 days** to initiate, **47 days** to implement and **100 days** to close/check effectiveness9. For lower-risk **Pilot: Fast-Track CAPAs, sample ![][image7], MEASURED**, it lists initiation of **12 days**, implementation of **64 days**, effectiveness checking of **13 days**, and an overall mean of **270 calendar days**. It also cites estimated engineering-hour savings of **64-75%** and up to **80%** shorter improvement implementation9. Using a projected 80:20 fast-track/external allocation, MDIC's **projected weighted average, an ESTIMATE derived from MEASURED data**, is given as **130 calendar days**, **65%** below the 379-day baseline, with **19 days** to initiate, **37 days** to implement and **84 days** to check effectiveness/close9. These component assignments and pilot totals are preserved as claims in the original research; the companion synthesis explicitly identifies the chart-reading errors and supplies corrected values.<br>
**FDA Warning Letters from 2025-2026, MEASURED**, also illustrate lengthy medical-device CAPA work. At **Envoy Medical, Inc.**, warning letter CMS #718762 of 11 November 2025, the FDA noted that an investigation was incomplete at the end of inspection on 2 July 2025, approximately **7 months / 210 calendar days** after the initial complaint71. At **Noah Medical Corporation**, warning letter CMS #702414 of 9 April 2025, inspectors found that 2 of 17 sampled CAPAs failed to identify a root cause. **CAPA 23-005**, opened on **14 April 2023**, concerned holes in sterile bronchoscope pouches during aging tests. **CAPA 24-007**, opened on **11 September 2024**, did not adequately investigate lot-to-lot variation. The original report connects these to broader **CAPA 24-028**, ongoing in April 2025, and infers approximately **24 months / 726 calendar days** without a target completion date72. That inferred 726-day open duration is excluded in the companion synthesis because the letter does not establish it. At **Medline Industries, LP**, warning letter CMS #723866 of 25 March 2026, complaint rates per million products reportedly exceeded limits over **3 consecutive quarters, Q1-Q3 2025**, approximately **9 months / 270 calendar days**, without reopening or supplementing CAPA as the SOP required54.<br>
Two medical-device **sample-data / benchmark ESTIMATE** sources provide additional reference figures. **Formly.ai** has a 2024 register of ![][image8] CAPAs for software-enabled medical devices, SaMD / glucose monitoring, with an average **98 calendar days** from initiation to verification, **18 calendar days** from verification to closure, and **116 calendar days** overall. Durations range from 60 days for CAPA-2024-001, 15 January-15 March 2024, to 128 days for CAPA-2024-004, 5 May-10 September 202440. **Elevate-CAPA Scorecard**, sample data for ![][image2] CAPAs closed over 12 months, shows a **median of 13 months / approximately 395 calendar days** from initiation through successful effectiveness verification8. Neither sample dataset establishes actual industry performance. Consultants and QMS tools describe common internal manufacturer targets of **30-60 calendar days**6, while a mean or median exceeding **90 calendar days**, or records open for over **18 months / approximately 540 days**, is described as an early warning of potential FDA Form 483 findings39.

### **5. Pharmaceuticals, Rail, Appliances, Contract Manufacturing, and Digitalization / AI Cases**

For **pharmaceuticals**, the reviewed material contains **no peer-reviewed measured average specifically covering a complete pharmaceutical CAPA/8D closure cycle**. The original report attributes to a **2025 LNS Research benchmark**, in a context where 25% of firms still tracked work manually, a cross-industry manufacturing/life-sciences reduction from **over 60 days to 15-20 days** after adopting electronic quality management systems (eQMS)76. The companion synthesis reclassifies this specific figure as a vendor claim. The *2023 EHS 4.0 Benchmark* and **LNS Research** manufacturing/pharmaceutical studies, including a November 2022 global survey validating ![][image1] of 385 responses, report **30-40% shorter CAPA closure cycles**, or **35% faster closure**, and **25% fewer audit findings** within a year after CAPA/EHS automation58. **Xavier Health** and **McKinsey** AI GxP materials (VENDOR CLAIM) describe reducing a pharmaceutical CAPA/change-control activity from **5 days to 1 day**, and cite McKinsey's estimated potential for up to **90%** shorter closure43. As a monitoring ESTIMATE, **Compliance Architects** recommends at least **6 months / 180 calendar days** of effectiveness monitoring for noncritical pharmaceutical CAPAs and **1 year / 365 calendar days** for critical CAPAs before full closure79. **Qualityze** cites a respiratory-device manufacturer reducing deviations by **40% within 6 months** after including Maintenance and Purchasing in CAPA triage meetings44. For related biotechnology change control, **f2i.bio** gives median targets below **21 days** for minor process changes and **60 days** for major changes80.<br>
For **rail, appliances and contract manufacturing**, the reviewed literature contains **no separately published MEASURED industry-average cycle time**. Contract and appliance manufacturers follow OEM customer schedules. A typical industrial DEADLINE framework cited here allows **24 hours** for team formation and containment D1-D3, **by day 8** for root-cause confirmation and corrective-action selection D4-D5, **by day 15** for implementation and validation of permanent corrective action D6, and **by day 30** for horizontal deployment (*Yokoten*) and closure D7-D8, followed by **90 days** of effectiveness monitoring and CAPA sustainment auditing81.<br>
By geography, covering **India, Germany, China and Vietnam**, and digitalization/AI case studies, an empirical study described as published in **India in April 2026** (MEASURED in the original report) examines multi-objective AI team formation at D2 for pulley fettling defects across ![][image8] detailed 8D projects. Manual selection reportedly took **1.8 days**, with 84.1% expertise coverage and a 7.1/10 team-effectiveness score, while the fully manual 8D cycle took **63 calendar days**. AI used only at D2 reduced formation to **38 minutes**, with 97.2% expertise coverage, a 23% smaller team of 6 and an 8.4/10 effectiveness score. Total 8D duration, with D1 and D3-D8 still manual, fell from **63 to 39 calendar days**, a **38.1%** improvement59. This study remains unverified in the companion synthesis. Also in India, **ERPDrive's 2026 report** (VENDOR CLAIM) asserts a reduction in 8D response from **5 days to under 8 hours**, and an 80% narrower product-recall scope82. For **Germany**, the original report cites Volkswagen's **10-working-day** 8D deadline and Continental's **2-working-day** D1-D3 deadline15; the Volkswagen completion/update distinction is corrected in the companion synthesis. **No collected empirical study reports separately measured 8D cycle times at plants in Vietnam or China.** In other industrial settings (VENDOR CLAIM), **iFactory** describes 12 months of biogas-plant data showing mean CAPA closure falling from **34 to 8 days**, a **76%** reduction83. For NCR/SCAR generally, it describes paper processes taking **40-90 days**, initial processing **5-15 days**, supplier 8D **30-90 days** plus effectiveness checks at **30/60/90 days**, and a SCAR response target below **30 days**; digitized NCR closure is reported at **8-20 days**45. **Oxmaint**, in healthcare/hospital compliance under Joint Commission / NABH / CMS, reports mean CAPA closure falling from **47 to 15 days**, a **68.1%** reduction84. **eLeap Software / QA Manager** QMS cases report reductions from **45 to 30 days**85 or **45 to 18 days**86.

## **Detailed Analysis: Overdue Rates, Recurrence and Time Bottlenecks Across D0-D8**

### **1. 8D and CAPA Records Overdue or Open Beyond 30, 60 and 90 Days**

MDIC's empirical duration distributions for two independent samples, ![][image9] baseline records and ![][image10] pilot records, provide quantitative MEASURED evidence on durations exceeding 30, 60, 90, 120, 150 and 180 days9. In the traditional baseline system, ![][image9], **28 records / 9.27%** closed in 0-30 days; **12 / 3.97%** in 31-60; **17 / 5.63%** in 61-90; **16 / 5.30%** in 91-120; **14 / 4.64%** in 121-150; **17 / 5.63%** in 151-180; and **198 / 65.56%** took over 180 days9. Cumulative calculations therefore give **90.73% / 274 of 302** beyond **30 days**, **86.75% / 262 of 302** beyond **60 days**, **81.13% / 245 of 302** beyond **90 days**, and **65.56% / 198 of 302** beyond **180 days**9. For the risk-routed pilot, ![][image10], the original report reads the chart as **217 records / 39.24%** closing in 0-30 days; **75 / 13.56%** in 31-60; **110 / 19.89%** in 61-90; **60 / 10.85%** in 91-120; **39 / 7.05%** in 121-150; **31 / 5.61%** in 151-180; and **21 / 3.80%** beyond 180 days9. On that reading, cumulative proportions fall to **60.76% / 336 of 553** beyond 30 days, **47.20% / 261 of 553** beyond 60 days, and **27.31% / 151 of 553** beyond 90 days9. The report also notes MDIC's statement that approximately 60% of pilot CAPAs closed within 60 days; the companion synthesis identifies the inconsistency with the chart reading and does not use the uncertain middle bins.

| **0-30 days** | 28 CAPAs (9.27%)9 | **90.73% (274/302)** beyond 30 days9 | 217 CAPAs (39.24%)9 | **60.76% (336/553)** beyond 30 days9 |
| **31-60 days** | 12 CAPAs (3.97%)9 | **86.75% (262/302)** beyond 60 days9 | 75 CAPAs (13.56%)9 | **47.20% (261/553)** beyond 60 days; approximately 60% closed in ![][image11] days9 |
| **61-90 days** | 17 CAPAs (5.63%)9 | **81.13% (245/302)** beyond 90 days9 | 110 CAPAs (19.89%)9 | **27.31% (151/553)** beyond 90 days9 |
| **91-120 days** | 16 CAPAs (5.30%)9 | **75.50% (228/302)** beyond 120 days9 | 60 CAPAs (10.85%)9 | **16.46% (91/553)** beyond 120 days9 |
| **121-150 days** | 14 CAPAs (4.64%)9 | **70.86% (214/302)** beyond 150 days9 | 39 CAPAs (7.05%)9 | **9.40% (52/553)** beyond 150 days9 |

MDIC also shows substantial differences by plant size. At large sites with more than 1,000 full-time staff, ![][image12], approximately **60%** of CAPAs closed within 60 days, leaving approximately **40%** beyond 60 days. At medium sites with 100-1,000 staff, ![][image13], only approximately **15%** closed within 60 days, leaving approximately **85%** beyond 60 days, which the report associates with limited dedicated engineering resources9. **Elevate-CAPA Scorecard's sample dataset**, ![][image2], ESTIMATE, defines closure as completed effectiveness verification: **43% (![][image14])** complete within ![][image11] months, **35% (![][image15])** take **12-18 months**, and **22% (![][image16])** take **over 18 months / 540 days**, so **57%** exceed 365 days8. Its nominal on-time performance is nevertheless **92%**, with only **8%** late. The analysis explains that many systems measure against the current due date after an approved extension, making a record that missed its original deadline appear on time. A CAPA can also count as on time even if half its component actions were late8. In manufacturing, **Jodoo** (VENDOR CLAIM) cites **38%** of open 8Ds at an automotive plant stalled at an approval or analysis step, and a **40% reduction** in overdue corrective actions after digitization46.

### **2. Recurrence After 8D/CAPA Closure and Global Audit Evidence**

Recurrence or repeat rate reflects the quality of root-cause analysis D4 and effectiveness verification D6-D7. In **MDIC's measured dataset**, ![][image5], the repeat CAPA rate was **16%**, falling to **0.4%** after the risk-tiered pilot framework, ![][image1]9. Consulting benchmarks compiled by **Certainty Software** (ESTIMATE) place mature CAPA/8D programs below **10% recurrence**, versus **30-50%** for organizations without formal effectiveness checks or closing records immediately after action implementation39. **Elevate-CAPA Scorecard sample data** (ESTIMATE) show **86% first-time effectiveness**, meaning **14%** failed the first effectiveness check because the issue recurred8. The original report classifies **LNS Research** as MEASURED / industry benchmark and states that **70% of CAPA programs fail** because of weak root-cause analysis77; it also reports **35% fewer repeat nonconformities** in organizations with integrated QMS platforms than in those using disconnected spreadsheets87.<br>
Official **IATF Global Oversight** MEASURED audit statistics across rolling 12-month periods from 2022-2026 provide broad evidence of automotive problem-solving weaknesses. **Clause 10.2.3, Problem solving**, is consistently the leading **major nonconformity**. Its share rises overall from **9.42% in August 2022** and **9.33% in January 2023** to **10.72% in March 2025**, **11.27% in June 2025**, **11.92% in December 2025**, **11.86% in April 2026** and **12.10% in August 2026**12. Including **clause 10.2.1, Nonconformity and corrective action**, which ranked first in January-October 2020 with 1,221 major findings and is described by the report as second across 2022-2026, brings the combined share to **17.70% of major nonconformities** in August 2026 across a global population of more than 104,000 automotive sites12. In US medical devices in 2025, **CAPA under 21 CFR 820.100** is described as the leading cited deficiency across **54 FDA Warning Letters**, ahead of Design Controls, 21 CFR 820.30, appearing in **26/54 letters / 48.1%**, and Complaint Handling, 21 CFR 820.198, appearing in **25/54 / 46.3%**. One cited example is Beta Bionics closing 31 of more than 500 insulin-cartridge leakage complaints without investigation54.

### **3. Time Bottlenecks: Which Steps Take Longest, and Why?**

Stage-level analysis identifies three structural bottlenecks rather than an even distribution of time. The original report identifies **effectiveness validation and closure, D6 validation / D7-D8 / CAPA effectiveness checks**, as the largest calendar-time component. Using its original MDIC chart assignments, ![][image5], it gives **221 of 379 days / 58.3%** for effectiveness checks and closure, and **100 of 167 days / 59.9%** in the External CAPA pilot, ![][image6]9. The companion synthesis corrects those chart assignments and totals. The underlying operational constraint is the observation window needed to establish nonrecurrence with objective data: at least **3 consecutive defect-free production batches**46, **2 complete preventive-maintenance cycles**95, or PPM/scrap monitoring over **30, 60, 90 or 180 days**, extending to **6-12 months** in pharmaceuticals39. At D7-D8, quality managers also spend time obtaining email/paper approvals and updating FMEA, Control Plans and SOPs. The report identifies a recurring IATF major nonconformity when shop-floor improvements are implemented but the Control Plan is rarely reviewed or updated after initial creation7.<br>
The second bottleneck, representing the greatest engineering workload, is **root-cause investigation and permanent corrective-action implementation, D4-D6**. The original MDIC reading gives **131 days / 34.6%** for investigation and implementation9, while the SaMD sample register, ![][image8], assigns **98 of 116 days / 84.5%** to initiation through verification, compared with 18 days for closure40. Semiconductor final physical failure analysis alone can require **22 working days**, followed by **14 working days** for the RCCA plan10. The report identifies three delay mechanisms. First, fragmented production data: when production orders, maintenance history and material-lot traceability reside in separate systems, engineers can spend days or weeks tracing a defect; complete data capture at intake is said to reduce cycle time by up to **40%** by eliminating repeated clarification77. Second, design changes, replacement tooling, process revalidation or shelf-life testing can take months8. Third is the **"30-Day Trap"**, creating **"Zombie Risk"**41. A rigid KPI demanding average CAPA/8D closure in **under 30 days**, without distinguishing early scope lock during the first 5 days from execution, can pressure engineers to stop at the first plausible 5 Whys answer. They may record "human error / retrain second-shift operators" to meet the deadline instead of investigating heater-block temperature drift requiring process revalidation. Both the occurrence cause and the escape point can then be missed, and the defect can recur after the short monitoring window7.<br>
The third bottleneck is **initiation, triage and cross-functional team formation, D0-D2**, which can influence downstream performance. In MDIC baseline data, ![][image5], waiting for the quality review/material review board, QRB/MRB, to classify and initiate CAPA takes an average of **43 calendar days**9. The original report interprets the 2026 Indian team-formation study as demonstrating an indirect causal relationship between team quality at D1/D2 and total D1-D8 duration. Manual selection took only **1.8 days**, but subjective membership selection achieved 84.1% expertise coverage, reportedly leading investigation in the wrong direction at D4 and a **63-day** total cycle. AI selected a six-person team with 97.2% coverage in **38 minutes**, and the overall process, with D3-D8 still manual, reportedly shortened by **24 days, from 63 to 39 days**59. The companion synthesis retains this study as unverified.

## **Original Consolidated Conclusions (MEASURED and DEADLINE Classifications)**

These conclusions translate the original report. They preserve its claims and classifications for traceability; the companion synthesis corrects or excludes several figures and should guide presentation use.

> 1. In automotive manufacturing, where IATF 16949 requires problem solving across **104,216 certified sites as of 20 December 2025**, and in industrial manufacturing, OEM DEADLINE requirements call for D3 containment within **24 hours to 2 working days**. The original report lists 8D submission/closure milestones of **10 working days** for Volkswagen, **10 days** for Grupo Segura, **14 working days** for KSR, **15 calendar days** for Ford, and **30-40 calendar days** for GM. It contrasts these with case-study MEASURED claims of **63 calendar days** manually, falling to **41 calendar days** after process improvement or **39 calendar days** when AI optimized D2 team formation from **1.8 days to 38 minutes**, and approximately **120 calendar days** to eliminate a production-line defect1. The companion synthesis corrects the Volkswagen milestone and excludes or leaves unverified the 63/41/39-day claims.<br>
> 2. For medical devices, MDIC's MEASURED baseline sample, ![][image5], has an overall mean of **379 calendar days**. The original chart reading assigns **43 days** to initiation, **131 days** to implementation and **221 days** to effectiveness checks/closure, followed by **167 calendar days** for external CAPAs, ![][image6], and **270 calendar days** for fast-track CAPAs, ![][image7]. It also cites FDA Warning Letters from 2025-2026 concerning incomplete work or unresolved trends over approximately **7 months / 210 days**, **3 quarters / 270 days**, and **24 months / 726 days**9. The companion synthesis corrects MDIC's component/pilot assignments and excludes the inferred 726-day duration.<br>
> 3. For aerospace under AS13000, defence and semiconductors, **no industry-wide MEASURED average total 8D closure time** is available. DEADLINE milestones require aerospace/defence containment within **24 hours to 2 days**, as cited for Barnes Aerospace, Safran and Lockheed Martin / Derco; ordinary nonconformity reporting within **5 working days** for Derco; and an 8D corrective-action plan or the cited closure rule within **30 calendar days**. Silicon Labs milestones are **7 working days** for initial failure analysis, **5 working days** for D3 containment, **22 working days** for final analysis, and **14 working days** for a D4-D5 corrective-action plan, totaling **36 working days** before D6-D8 implementation10. The original report's attribution of these FAQ deadlines to JESD671 is not verified by the companion synthesis.<br>
> 4. Pharmaceuticals, rail, appliances and contract manufacturing have **no separately published empirical MEASURED industry-average 8D duration from complaint receipt to closure** in the reviewed academic material. The original report cites a cross-industry LNS Research claim of CAPA automation reducing closure from **over 60 days to 15-20 days**, with **30-40%** shorter cycles, and describes IATF audit nonconformity closure as limited to **90 calendar days**14. The companion synthesis reclassifies the 60-to-15/20-day claim as VENDOR CLAIM and clarifies that 90 days is the certification body's decision deadline.<br>
> 5. In MDIC's baseline closed-CAPA sample, ![][image9], **90.7% (274/302)** took over 30 days, **86.8% (262/302)** over 60 days, **81.1% (245/302)** over 90 days and **65.6% (198/302)** over 180 days. The original pilot chart reading, ![][image10], gives **60.8%**, **47.2%**, **27.3%** and **3.8%**, respectively; the middle-bin interpretation is flagged as uncertain in the companion synthesis. Reported recurrence fell from **16% to 0.4%**. The original report also cites LNS Research's **70%** CAPA-program failure claim due to weak RCA and IATF clause **10.2.3, Problem solving**, at **12.10%** of global major nonconformities in August 20269.
